title: The .NET Regex API
summary: IsMatch, Match and NextMatch, Matches, Count, EnumerateMatches, Split and Replace: which call to make, what each one costs, and why you build a Regex once.

steps.title: One pattern, many questions
body: `System.Text.RegularExpressions.Regex` answers different questions with different methods. Pick the one that
asks exactly what you need, because the cheaper questions do less work:
| Question | Call | Returns |
| Is there a match? | `regex.IsMatch(s)` | `bool` |
| What is the first match? | `regex.Match(s)`, then `m.NextMatch()` | `Match` (check `m.Success`) |
| Every match, with groups | `regex.Matches(s)` | `MatchCollection` |
| How many? (.NET 7+) | `regex.Count(s)` | `int` |
| Where, without allocating? (.NET 7+) | `regex.EnumerateMatches(s)` | `ValueMatch` per match |
| Cut the text apart | `regex.Split(s)` | `string[]` |
| Rewrite it | `regex.Replace(s, "...")` | `string` |
Below, each match of `key=number` is highlighted with its two named groups. `mode=fast` has no number, so it
is not a match. In C# you would read the groups with `m.Groups["key"].Value`.

steps.prompt: `Match` gives the first match; `NextMatch` continues from where it ended. What does this print?
steps.explain: `Index` is the zero-based position where the match starts. When there are no more matches, `NextMatch` returns a `Match` whose `Success` is false (never null), which ends the loop.

steps.title: Settings as key=value
prompt: A config line holds settings like `retries=3 timeout=30`. Write a pattern with two named groups, `key` (a word)
and `value` (digits), that finds every numeric setting. Settings with a non-numeric value, like `mode=fast`, are
steps.explain: In C#: `foreach (Match m in regex.Matches(line)) settings[m.Groups["key"].Value] = int.Parse(m.Groups["value"].Value);`

steps.title: Matches, Count and EnumerateMatches
body: `Matches` returns a `MatchCollection` that is **lazy**: no matching happens until you enumerate it. Asking for
its `.Count` forces a scan of the whole input and creates a `Match` object (with its groups) for every hit.
Since .NET 7 there are two cheaper calls for hot paths:
```csharp fragment
var digits = new Regex(@"[0-9]+");
int n = digits.Count(line);                     // how many, no Match objects at all
foreach (ValueMatch m in digits.EnumerateMatches(line))
ReadOnlySpan<char> number = line.AsSpan(m.Index, m.Length);   // where: Index and Length only
total += int.Parse(number);
`ValueMatch` has only `Index` and `Length`: no `Value` string and no groups. That is the trade: zero
allocations in exchange for slicing the input yourself. The enumerator is a `ref struct`, so it cannot be used
with LINQ or kept across an `await`. When you need groups, use `Matches`.

steps.prompt: A service counts `ERROR` lines in a 2 GB log, line by line, with a `Regex` built once. Which call does the least work per line?
steps.explain: `Count` (.NET 7+) only counts: it never builds a `Match`, a `Group` or a substring. `Matches(...).Count` gets the same number but allocates an object per match. `Split` builds strings for all the text in between. If you only need yes or no, `IsMatch` is cheaper still.

steps.prompt: `Split` cuts the text at every match. What does this print?
steps.explain: When the pattern has a capturing group, .NET puts the captured text into the result too, between the pieces. That is handy for keeping separators, and a surprise when you only added brackets for grouping. Use `(?:...)` to group without capturing.

steps.title: Split a messy list
prompt: Users type tag lists like `a, b,c ;d`: commas or semicolons, with or without spaces around them. Write a
pattern for `Regex.Split` that returns just the tags, with no spaces and no empty entries.
hints: The separator is one comma or semicolon, `[,;]`, with optional whitespace on both sides.
`\s*[,;]\s*`, and no capturing groups, or the separators end up in the result.
steps.explain: Putting the spaces inside the separator is what keeps them out of the tags. A space alone is not a separator here, so `two words` stays one tag.

steps.prompt: Complete the allocation-free loop that adds up every number in `line`.
steps.explain: `EnumerateMatches` yields `ValueMatch` values, which carry only `Index` and `Length`. There is no `Value`: you slice the span yourself.

steps.title: Sum the numbers without allocating
prompt: Write `int SumNumbers(string text)`: the sum of every run of ASCII digits in `text`. `a1 b22 c333` gives 356.
Use `EnumerateMatches` and parse each number from a span, so no `Match` objects or substrings are created.
Use `[0-9]+`, not `\d+`: `\d` also matches digits from other scripts (like `٣`), which `int.Parse` rejects.
template: Dojo.Eq("a1 b22 c333", 356, SumNumbers("a1 b22 c333"));
Dojo.Eq("a minus sign is not part of the number", 5, SumNumbers("x-5y"));
Dojo.Eq("Arabic-Indic digits are not ASCII digits", 7, SumNumbers("٣ and 7"));

steps.title: Build it once
body: Creating a `Regex` **parses** the pattern and builds a matcher. With `RegexOptions.Compiled` it also generates
IL at run time, which costs far more (often a millisecond or more). Doing that per call is a classic hot spot.
- `new Regex(...)` is **never cached**. Build it once and keep it: a `private static readonly Regex` field.
- The **static** methods (`Regex.IsMatch(input, pattern)`) keep a small cache of recently used patterns,
`Regex.CacheSize`, 15 by default. Fine for a handful of constant patterns; more than 15 in a hot path and
they are parsed again and again.
- A `Regex` is immutable and **thread-safe**: one instance can serve every request at once.
```csharp
static class TicketKeys
private static readonly Regex Key = new(@"\b[A-Z]{2,5}-[0-9]+\b", RegexOptions.Compiled);
public static bool Has(string s) => Key.IsMatch(s);
For a fixed pattern, the next lesson's `[GeneratedRegex]` is better still: the work happens at build time.

steps.prompt: Is the regex usage fine as written, or should it be built once (or generated)?
items: `Regex.IsMatch(arg, @"^--\w+")` once, when a CLI tool starts
`new Regex(p, RegexOptions.Compiled)` inside an ASP.NET request handler
`new Regex(@"[0-9]+")` inside a loop over a million lines
A `private static readonly Regex` field used by every request
Static `Regex.Match` calls with 40 different constant patterns in a hot path
steps.explain: One-off use costs nothing worth fixing. Construction per call, and more distinct static patterns than `Regex.CacheSize` (15), parse the same pattern over and over.

steps.title: Symptom: CPU at 90% in the ticket service
prompt: **Symptom.** After a release, the ticket service's p99 latency went from 8 ms to 400 ms and CPU sits at 90%.
The profiler's flame graph is dominated by `RegexCompiler`, `DynamicMethod` and `RegexParser.Parse`, all
The results are correct; the cost is not. Fix `TicketParser` so the regex is built **once** and shared by
every call. Keep `RegexOptions.Compiled`: it pays off once the regex is reused.
solution: private static readonly Regex Key = new(@"\b[A-Z]{2,5}-[0-9]+\b", RegexOptions.Compiled);
template: Dojo.Eq("finds both keys", new List<string> { "OPS-311", "PAY-7" }, TicketParser.Keys("fixes OPS-311 and PAY-7"));
Dojo.Eq("no keys in plain text", new List<string>(), TicketParser.Keys("nothing to see"));
for (var i = 0; i < 200; i++) dojoTotal += TicketParser.Keys($"request {i}: OPS-{i}").Count;
Dojo.Eq("200 requests, one key each", 200, dojoTotal);

require.message: Keeps the Regex in a static readonly field

hints: Move the `new Regex(...)` out of the method into a field of the class.
`private static readonly Regex Key = new(@"...", RegexOptions.Compiled);` and use `Key.Matches(text)` in the method.
steps.explain: Each `new Regex(..., RegexOptions.Compiled)` parsed the pattern and emitted IL on every request. A static readonly field does that once per process, and the instance is safe to share across threads. The analyzer `SYSLIB1045` would also point at this line and suggest `[GeneratedRegex]`.
